title: Perfect knowledge
hookLine: the night of awakening, told in verse (Buddhacarita 14)

cards: The noise is over. Mara's army, the arrows, the shrieking shapes, is gone. What's left is a man under a tree, and a night ahead of him.
A story could stop here, with the victory. The poem doesn't. It slows down and walks through the dark one stretch at a time, the way someone who can't sleep feels every hour of a long night.
The battle was loud. The awakening, in Ashvaghosha's telling, is quiet, and it takes all night.

teach.h: FIRST WATCH: HIS OWN PAST LIVES.
teach.b: First, he looks back. In the first watch of the night, the poem says, he remembers his own former lives, one after another: where he was born, what his name was, what happened to him.
What he feels, looking back, is not pride. It's compassion, for every being caught in that long turning. Second, he looks out.

teach.h: MIDDLE WATCH: ALL BEINGS, COMING AND GOING.
teach.b: In the middle watch, the poem gives him a clear, divine sight. He sees beings everywhere dying and being born again, rising and falling according to what they have done.
The whole world seems to him to have no solid core, like the stem of a plantain plant: layers, with nothing hard in the middle. Third, he looks in.

teach.h: LAST WATCH: THE CHAIN OF CAUSES.
teach.b: In the last watch, he asks the question under all the others: where do old age and death come from? From birth. And birth?

From becoming. Link by link, he follows the chain back to not knowing, ignorance. Then he sees it the other way: when ignorance ends, the chain comes apart, link by link, all the way to the end of old age and death.
As the night ends, the poem says, he reaches perfect knowledge. He has become the Buddha, the awakened one. The earth sways, flowers fall, and the gods rejoice.
At the center of all that color sits one still figure who has finished a long question. The discourses tell this night more plainly, with the same three watches. The poem adds the beauty.
Both share the shape: looking back, looking out, looking in, and then light.

how: The awakening is remembered at Vesak (or Wesak), when in many places temples are lit and people gather to meditate, keep precepts and hear teachings; in some places devotees sit through the night in memory of the night under the tree.

o: knowing every fact there is to know
a secret he learned from his old teachers
the full understanding he reached at dawn

games.q: the night of awakening: tap the pairs.

s: in the poem, the awakening happens the moment Mara runs away
the poem walks through a whole night of watches before the dawn.
looking back on his past lives, he feels compassion
the poem says compassion, for every being caught in that turning.
in the last watch he traces old age and death back to ignorance
link by link, and then sees the chain come apart when ignorance ends.

games.q: you've just faced down an army of fears. it's dark, and you're still under the tree. what do you do?
o: get up and celebrate the victory.
stay seated and keep looking, all night.
go and find your old companions.
games.why: he stays. the poem gives the whole night to remembering, seeing and understanding, and the awakening comes at dawn.

practice: For a few breaths, look back over today, what happened, without judging it. Then look out at the people around you, near and far, each going through their own day, and then look in, at just this breath, coming and going.

wordCard.voice: Perfect knowledge. Through the watches of one night he remembers, sees and understands, and at dawn he is the Buddha. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: the night of knowing. Back, out, in, and then the dawn. Day seven hundred seventeen, done.

sources.ref: Buddhacarita 14 (the watches of the night, dependent origination, the awakening at dawn)
Majjhima Nikaya 36 (the three knowledges in the three watches)
